title: QuestDB 10.2: commits that survive a power loss
summary: QuestDB 10.2 adds power-loss durability for WAL tables, GROUPING SETS, passthrough views with row-level retention, and a DEDUP SKIP mode that keeps the first copy of a row.
body_markdown:
QuestDB is the open-source time-series database for demanding workloads—from trading floors to mission control. It delivers ultra-low latency, high ingestion throughput, and a multi-tier storage engine. Native support for Parquet and SQL keeps your data portable, AI-ready—no vendor lock-in.


---


QuestDB 10.2 is out, and most of what's new replaces something people have been working around. Choosing between fast commits and commits that survive a power loss. Writing one query per level of a report and adding up the totals somewhere else. Repeating the same filter in every query against a table that holds more than the application wants to see. Having a resent row overwrite the one that arrived first.


Here's what's new:


**Power-loss durability for WAL tables** , enabled with` cairo.commit.mode=adaptive` , makes commits survive an operating system crash or a power loss, for much less than` sync` costs. Each commit flushes only its write-ahead log files, and the table files are flushed once a minute. It's opt-in.


**GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE** return detail rows, subtotals and a grand total from one query and one scan, with` GROUP BY` or` SAMPLE BY` .


**Passthrough views and EXPIRE ROWS** : a materialized view can now be a filtered copy of a table (` SELECT ... WHERE` ), kept up to date as rows arrive.` EXPIRE ROWS` adds row-level retention on top, so the view keeps only the last hour, the outages that are still in effect, or the latest reading per device.


**DEDUP SKIP** keeps the first row written for a key and discards later copies, the counterpart of` UPSERT` .


The release also brings faster ingestion of small QWP messages, WAL apply fixes and a long list ofother changes . If you only need the summary, readbefore you upgrade and go togetting 10.2 .


---


## Commits that survive a power loss


By default, QuestDB doesn't wait for the disk before acknowledging a commit, so an operating system crash or a power loss can lose the latest commits and leave table files damaged. Adaptive durability mode protects WAL tables from both:


server.conf


```text
cairo.commit.mode=adaptive
```


Each commit flushes only its own WAL files. The table files are flushed once a minute, and after a crash QuestDB rebuilds them from the WAL, so it restarts with every table consistent instead of tripping over damaged files.


- **Pair it with durable acks.** By default, commits share one flush every 50 ms, so a power loss can take the commits acknowledged in that window. With` request_durable_ack=local` , QWP clients keep each batch until the server confirms it's on the disk, and resend it after a reconnect.` cairo.adaptive.commit.group.window=0` makes every commit wait for its own flush instead.
- **What it costs:** each commit waits for a flush, so it's slower than the default, but costs much less than` sync` . Larger batches and concurrent writers spread the cost.
- **What it doesn't cover:** non-WAL tables, or losing the disk itself.


The[durability docs](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/durability/) have the details.


---


## Subtotals and grand totals with GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE


A desk report wants volume per currency pair and venue, a subtotal per pair, and a grand total.[ROLLUP](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/grouping-sets/#rollup) returns all three levels from one query, in a single scan:


Volume per pair and venue, with subtotals and a total


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20symbol%2C%20ecn%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20round(sum(quantity)%20%2F%201e6)%20AS%20volume_m%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20count()%20AS%20trades%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20GROUPING_ID(symbol%2C%20ecn)%20AS%20level%0AFROM%20fx_trades%0AWHERE%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A%20%20AND%20symbol%20IN%20(%27EURUSD%27%2C%20%27GBPUSD%27)%0AGROUP%20BY%20ROLLUP(symbol%2C%20ecn)%0AORDER%20BY%20level%2C%20symbol%2C%20ecn%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT symbol, ecn,          round(sum(quantity) / 1e6) AS volume_m,          count() AS trades,          GROUPING_ID(symbol, ecn) AS level   FROM fx_trades   WHERE timestamp IN '$yesterday'     AND symbol IN ('EURUSD', 'GBPUSD')   GROUP BY ROLLUP(symbol, ecn)   ORDER BY level, symbol, ecn;
```


symbol ecn volume_m trades level


EURUSD Currenex 23052 171476 0


EURUSD EBS 23195 171920 0


EURUSD Hotspot 22991 170637 0


EURUSD LMAX 23273 173566 0


GBPUSD Currenex 18566 138731 0


GBPUSD EBS 18112 136053 0


GBPUSD Hotspot 18358 136658 0


GBPUSD LMAX 18433 137796 0


EURUSD null 92512 687599 1


GBPUSD null 73469 549238 1


null null 165981 1236837 3


A rolled-up column comes back as` NULL` , and` GROUPING_ID()` tells those rows apart from real` NULL` s: 0 is a detail row, 1 a subtotal and 3 the grand total.` CUBE` adds totals in every direction, and` GROUPING SETS` lists only the levels you want. With` SAMPLE BY 1h ROLLUP(ecn)` , every hour gets its own per-venue rows and total, and` FILL` works too.


Grouping sets don't use the vectorized` GROUP BY` path, so for a single-key` sum()` a` UNION ALL` of plain` GROUP BY` queries can still be several times faster on many cores. They can't be used in materialized views. The[reference](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/grouping-sets/) has the details, and the cookbook has a[subtotals and grand totals recipe](https://questdb.com/docs/cookbook/sql/advanced/subtotals-and-grand-totals/) .

## Keeping only the rows you need with EXPIRE ROWS


A grid operator's console lists planned outages, and must only show the ones still in effect. A materialized view can't filter on` now()` , so until now every query needed its own` WHERE planned_end > now()` .


10.2 adds[passthrough views](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/materialized-views/#passthrough-views) , materialized views that copy their base table row for row, optionally narrowed to some columns or rows.[EXPIRE ROWS](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/expire-rows/) attaches a policy to one, checked on every read:


Planned outages still in effect


```text
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW outages_active AS (     SELECT * FROM planned_outages   ) EXPIRE ROWS WHEN planned_end < now();
```


Outages drop out of` outages_active` as they end. A condition on the designated timestamp, such as` WHEN timestamp < dateadd('h', -1, now())` , keeps a rolling window.` KEEP LATEST PARTITION BY robot_id` gives a fleet dashboard each robot's latest status, and` KEEP 10 HIGHEST ON vibration PARTITION BY turbine_id` the ten worst readings per turbine.


Only a` WHEN` condition on the designated timestamp frees disk. The others hide rows from queries, and` KEEP` policies rank the whole view on every read: in the PR's test, one day of a 20-million-row view took 7.2 ms to read without a policy and 5.0 s with` KEEP 2 HIGHEST` . Other materialized and live views can't read a view that has a policy.


---


## DEDUP SKIP: keep the first copy of a row


Field gateways buffer sensor readings while they're offline, and resend everything since their last confirmed upload when they reconnect, including readings the server already has. With` DEDUP UPSERT` , every resent reading replaces the stored one, so a` received_at` column that recorded when each reading first arrived now shows the resend. The new[SKIP mode](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/deduplication/#upsert-and-skip-modes) keeps the first row and discards later ones, like` INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` :


Keep the first delivery of each reading


```text
CREATE TABLE readings (       timestamp TIMESTAMP,       sensor_id SYMBOL,       temperature DOUBLE,       humidity DOUBLE,       received_at TIMESTAMP   ) TIMESTAMP(timestamp) PARTITION BY DAY   DEDUP SKIP KEYS(timestamp, sensor_id);
```


An existing table switches with` ALTER TABLE ... DEDUP ENABLE SKIP KEYS(...)` , without rewriting stored rows.` SKIP` doesn't compare columns outside the key, and a commit that holds only duplicates leaves the partition untouched, Parquet partitions included.` UPSERT` got faster at the same case: resending unchanged rows into a Parquet partition no longer rewrites it.


---


## Other changes


- **Small QWP messages.** One-row messages ingest at about 3.9 million rows per second, up from about 210,000, on one connection with 12 cores and tmpfs. 1,000-row messages are unchanged.
- **WAL apply.** A backlog of small out-of-order transactions over a wide time range no longer makes WAL apply fall back to one transaction at a time and fall behind. Idle QWP connections no longer block WAL cleanup.
- **Parquet indexes.** Partitions written by 9.3.4 to 10.0.1 could have indexes that miss rows. Queries over them now fail instead of returning wrong rows, most are repaired automatically, and[FORCE REINDEX PARQUET](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/alter-table-force-reindex-parquet/) repairs the rest online.
- **Fixes** in` WINDOW JOIN` , set operations,` SAMPLE BY` with` FILL` ,` RIGHT` and` FULL` joins,` SPLICE JOIN` and materialized views, among others. See the[release notes page](https://questdb.com/release-notes/) .


---


## Before you upgrade


- **` DEDUP SKIP` .** Older releases treat a` SKIP` table as` UPSERT` without an error, so keep that in mind before using it if you might need to downgrade.
- **Materialized views.** The part of a view's query that reads its base table can't use` LIMIT` or a window function inside an expression. Existing views keep refreshing, but replaying their` SHOW CREATE` output fails. See the[restrictions](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/create-mat-view/#limit-and-window-function-restrictions) .
- **QWP senders** that send the designated timestamp twice, through` at()` and as a named column, are now rejected. They used to be accepted and stored wrong timestamps.
- **Parquet from 9.3.4 to 10.0.1.** If you used indexes on Parquet partitions, run[FORCE REINDEX PARQUET](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/alter-table-force-reindex-parquet/) on tables the compaction job doesn't repair.


Before upgrading, read the[upgrade checklist](https://questdb.com/docs/operations/upgrade/#before-you-upgrade) , which covers going back to an earlier release once 10.2 has run on a database.


---


## Getting 10.2


```text
docker pull questdb/questdb:10.2.0
```


Or[download QuestDB](https://questdb.com/download/) directly. The[full changelog is on GitHub](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/releases/tag/10.2.0) .


If you try power-loss durability on your own storage, or` DEDUP SKIP` on a feed that resends data, tell us how it goes on[Slack](https://slack.questdb.com/) or[Discourse](https://community.questdb.com/) .
